newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stoiber repeats demand for 3.0 EMU deficit target.
newsitem.headline: Stoiber repeats demand for 3.0 EMU deficit target.

text.p: Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber on Wednesday reiterated his demand for a strict interpretation of the budget deficit limit which is one of the criteria for joining Europe's planned single currency.

The Maastricht treaty calls for budget deficits to be limited to three percent of gross domestic product. Stoiber has whipped up a storm in Germany, struggling to met the target, by insisting this must mean 3.0 percent and no more.
He said the difference might not be decisive for economists, but it was for the majority of ordinary Germans.
"If we now move away from three it will shake people's confidence," Stoiber told national ARD television.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, bowing to pressure from German EMU hardliners like Stoiber, on Tuesday pledged Bonn would meet the 3.0 percent deficit goal in time for the punctual start of European monetary union (EMU).
Stoiber criticised the opposition Social Democrats and Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, accusing them of no longer taking the deficit target seriously.
He said the planned currency, the euro, would be a great opportunity but would also determine the future of its participants because a weak euro could lead to inflation.

Stoiber would not say if he thought Germany, weighed down by over four million unemployed and weak economic growth, would hit the deficit target in 1997 -- the year that counts for qualifying for EMU entry in 1999.
He insisted that meeting the convergence criteria was more important than sticking to the EMU timetable.

But Stoiber also told Kohl that it was not the policy of his party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) led by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, to make the future of the ruling coalition dependent on the issue of EMU targets.
The CSU is the Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats.
